kakekotoba.interaction: The falling of blossoms/snow (降る) is overlaid with the sense of the speaker's own aging and passing of years (経る/古る) — 'furi yuku' means both 'falling/scattering as it goes' and 'growing old as time passes,' fusing the image of petals blown by the storm with the speaker's own decline into age.

Not strictly a kakekotoba but a rhetorical negation ('not the snow, but...') that sets up the pivot from natural snow to the human referent; included for completeness though it is grammatical rather than homophonic.

bipartite.kami_theme: A storm scatters blossoms in the garden, and what falls resembles snow
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker realizes that what is truly 'falling'/'passing' is not snow but his own aging self
bipartite.pivot_note: The poem sets up an expectation — falling white things in a wind-torn garden must be snow — only to overturn it: the falling thing is revealed to be the speaker himself, i.e. his years and vitality declining. The kakekotoba on ふりゆく (falling / growing old) is the fulcrum of this revelation, collapsing the meteorological image and the human condition into a single verb.

kigo.note: 花 (hana) without qualification conventionally means cherry blossoms in the classical canon, the archetypal spring kigo; here it is being scattered by a storm (嵐), evoking the poignant late-spring image of blossoms falling, which the poem then likens to snow — a deliberate cross-seasonal illusion (blossoms mistaken for winter snow) that is common in courtly poetry to heighten pathos.
